News.title: Workers face having pay docked for calling in sick in Germany – where average employee takes over TWO WEEKS off a year
News.content:
SICKIE CRACKDOWN Workers face having pay docked for calling in sick in Germany – where average employee takes over TWO WEEKS off a year

WORKERS in Germany will want to think twice before ringing in sick as they could have sick pay slashed in a new crackdown to “toughen” the workforce.

It comes as employees in Germany take an average of 14.8 sick days per year – one of the highest in Europe.





Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s sick-leave smackdown hopes to beat the soaring numbers of workers taking days of work.

In his 2025 election campaign, Merz vowed to crack down on spiralling sick leave.

He was practically tearing his hair out at his country’s two-week sick leave rate.

In covert talks revealed by newspaper Bild, the ruling centre-Right Christian Democrats (CDU) party and their coalition partner are thinking of docking wages for workers calling in sick.

Under the new plans, workers who ring in sick five times or less could be rewarded with an extra day off.

The rate of sick leave is three times higher than the British average, which came in at around 4.4 days a year in 2024.

The wage-cutting proposals aim to stop workers taking days off for trivial sicknesses like colds.



Merz has previously lashed out at four-day work weeks and work-life balance as he warned Germans that they must work harder to support the country’s ailing economy.

What are sick leave rules in the UK? FROM April 6, workers in the UK are paid wages from the first day taken off for illness. Pay amounts to £123.25 per week, or 80 per cent of earnings if this is lower. Workers must notify employers and a sick note, issued by a doctor, is required for sick leave longer than seven days. Sick leave pay can be shelled out for up to 28 weeks of absence.

The CDU voted to ban workers from phoning in sick in order to boost productivity levels earlier this year.

Workers can be signed off work on sick leave for up to five days by speaking to their doctor on the phone and asking for a sick note.

However, the CDU have been pushing for employees to visit a doctor’s office in person to get signed off.

Germany’s trade union confederation has slammed the plans, as it puts workers “under suspicion” and encourages seniors to treat staff like “shirkers and slackers”.



It comes as Germany ups the ante in preparing to face off Russia.

New guidance from the government forbids working age German men from leaving the country for three months or more without permission from the German army.

Restricting the movements of men of fighting age comes as the country is preparing for a potential Russian attack on NATO within the next two to three years.

News.title: Sick thug who left girlfriend in wheelchair after hurling her from 40ft tower block laughs as he’s jailed
News.content:
HORROR PLUNGE Sick thug who left girlfriend in wheelchair after hurling her from 40ft tower block laughs as he’s jailed

A SICK thug who left his girlfriend with horror injuries after he hurled her from a 40ft tower block laughed as he was jailed today.

Bobbie Goodman, 18, was shoved four storeys to the ground below by Jordan Herring and was temporarily left in a wheelchair.





The teen miraculously landed on a grass verge in Solihull, West Midlands, and not a concrete path a couple of feet away that could have killed her.

Bobbie suffered life-changing injuries including a smashed spine, broken ribs, shattered pelvis and a collapsed lung.

Sickingly, Herring maintained that his then-girlfriend jumped – despite there being an hour’s wait before a 999 call was made.



The thug showed no remorse today as he was jailed for years and laughed as the sentence was handed down.

Herring, 22, was found guilty of unlawful wounding but was cleared of more serious offences of attempted murder and inflicting grievous bodily harm with intent.

He was also convicted of controlling and coercive behaviour against Bobbie after a campaign of abuse leading up to the push.

The court heard Herring had launched into the attack in a cannabis-fuelled rage after interrogating Bobbie about her Snapchat messages.



He had taken the teen to his mum’s house to evade her concerned family, who had been looking for her.

She was already “battered and bruised” with two black eyes and marks to her neck when she arrived at the tower block, it was said.

Shocking CCTV showed her plunging 40ft as Herring refused to give her CPR or call for help.

He also threatened his mum with a knife to prevent her calling emergency services, which she ultimately did not do for one hour and 20 minutes.

Herring then lied to the police – claiming Bobbie jumped from the window in a suicide attempt.



Recalling the horror, she told officers the thug held her near the window and threatened: “I will throw you out, I will kill you.”

In a victim impact statement, Bobbie, now 21, said: “What Herring did to me has affected me in many ways.

“I am extremely lucky to be alive.

News.title: Why is Trump blocking the Strait of Hormuz? What the Iran blockade actually means and why the UK isn’t involved
News.content:
DONALD Trump has launched a naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz – the narrow waterway a fifth of the world’s oil usually passes through every day.

The move has raised the stakes in the struggle for control over the essential energy chokepoint and risks putting the two-week ceasefire deal under even greater strain.





What is the Strait of Hormuz and why does it matter?

The Strait of Hormuz is the vital shipping lane a fifth of the world’s oil passes through.

President Donald Trump has been hell-bent on reopening it since Iran effectively closed it at the end of February.

The US Navy has cut off the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea east of the strait, preventing Iran from profiting off oil and gas exports.

US Central Command has warned that any Iranian-linked vessel daring to break into the waterway would be subject to “interception or capture”.

The blockade applies to all vessels, regardless of flag, though it will only be enforced “partially” on ships going to and from Iranian ports.

US Central Command confirmed: “The blockade will not impede neutral transit passage through the Strait of Hormuz to or from non-Iranian destinations.”

UK Maritime Trade Operations confirmed that neutral vessels will get a “limited grace period” to leave, but it didn’t specify for how long.



Why has Trump launched the blockade?

The blockade follows 21 hours of failed peace talks in Pakistan, where the US and Iran could not resolve their central disagreement – Tehran’s insistence that it will not completely abandon its nuclear programme.

This was the primary catalyst for Trump launching Operation Epic Fury in February.

Iran accused the US of arriving with “excessive demands” and “unlawful requests.”

Leaving Islamabad on Air Force Two, Vice President JD Vance said: “Do we see a fundamental commitment of will for the Iranians not to develop a nuclear weapon… for the long term? We haven’t seen that yet.”

Trump had already criticised Tehran for charging a $2million (£1.5million) fee on every oil tanker that passed through the strait.



He wrote on Truth Social: “Iran will not be allowed to profit off this Illegal Act of EXTORTION. They want money and, more importantly, they want Nuclear.”

Iran previously called the threat of a blockade “ridiculous and laughable”, with its Revolutionary Guard insisting the strait was within its control.

On Monday, April 13, the tone shifted, with a military spokesperson calling the restrictions “piracy” and warning that no Persian Gulf port would be safe for as long as the siege continues.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu threw his support behind Trump’s approach.

He told his cabinet: “The breakdown came from the American side, which could not tolerate Iran’s blatant violation of the terms for entering negotiations.



“The agreement was that there would be a ceasefire, and that the Iranians would immediately open the strait. They did not do so. The Americans could not accept this.”

After the blockade began, Trump returned to social media to warn: “Iran’s Navy is laying at the bottom of the sea, completely obliterated – 158 ships.

“What we have not hit are their small number of, what they call, ‘fast attack ships,’ because we did not consider them much of a threat.

“Warning: If any of these ships come anywhere close to our BLOCKADE, they will be immediately ELIMINATED, using the same system of kill that we use against the drug dealers on boats at Sea.



“It is quick and brutal. P.S. 98.2% of Drugs coming into the US by Ocean or Sea have STOPPED!”

Why is the UK not involved?

Prime Minister Keir Starmer has made clear that Britain will not be part of the blockade.

He said that the UK will not get “dragged in” to the conflict — a position that has put the special relationship between London and Washington under serious strain.

Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, Starmer said: “What we’ve been doing over the last few weeks – and this was part of what I was discussing with the Gulf states last week – is bringing countries together to keep the strait open, not shut.”

He added: “We’re not supporting the blockade and all of the marshalling diplomatically, politically and capability.



“We do have mine-sweeping capability, I won’t go into operational matters, but we do have that capability – that’s all focused, from our point of view, on getting the strait fully open.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Following the failed peace talks, sources told the Wall Street Journal that Trump is weighing up a return to military strikes.

Trump told Fox News: “I would hate to do it, but it’s their water, their desalinization [sic] plants, their electric-generating plants, which are very easy to hit.”

News.title: Chilling clues that unlocked case of OAP stabbed in the neck & set alight…11 yrs after cops ruled death a freak accident
News.content:
TRAGIC MISTAKES Chilling clues that unlocked case of OAP stabbed in the neck & set alight…11 yrs after cops ruled death a freak accident

WHEN the body of widow Una Crown was found in the hallway of her bungalow, by her distraught niece Judith, police were called to the scene.

But, spotting a charred tea towel in the kitchen and burns to her body, officers concluded that the 86-year-old, from Wisbech, Cambridgeshire, had accidentally set herself alight on her oven and had probably suffered a heart attack.





Incredibly, wounds on her neck were put down to damage caused by her scarf tightening as she fell.

But just two days later, they realised they had made a huge mistake. The post mortem showed the popular former postmistress had been brutally stabbed to death with repeated strikes to her throat by a long-bladed knife.

By then, vital forensic evidence had been lost by emergency services and family touching objects at the crime scene and cleaning up.

“If you ‘lose a scene’ for a couple of days, as happened in 2013, you can lose some key evidence, and it’s difficult,” Det Supt Iain Moore, who led the cold case team, tells The Sun.

“It’s what is called the Golden Hour, which is the time immediately after the offence, where the evidence is rich.

“Forensic testing was still done back on the scene on the Tuesday after the murder but we just didn’t get a result back then. Whether or not we would have done, if the scene hadn’t been contaminated, is the million-dollar question.”

A police investigation threw up a list of suspects but, without the lost evidence, nothing could be proved against any of them.



Her killer walked free for 11 years until the case was re-opened in 2023 when advances in DNA technology, along with a re-examining of old interviews and fresh ones, eventually led the cold case team to a trusted neighbour.

A two-part Channel 4 special of 24 Hours in Police Custody, follows the dogged work of detectives who finally got justice for Una and her family.

“The guilty verdict was massive for the family,” says Iain. “They’re such a lovely family. They were hugely respectful to the team throughout the whole case, even taking into account the mistakes made in 2013.



“We were surprised at the decision, on the day. It was a collective one. There weren’t just police officers on the scene, there were paramedics and fire officers. Their hypothesis was that it was a non-suspicious death.

“Hindsight is a wonderful thing, but it’s just difficult to see how they came to that conclusion. However, that said, they did gain some crucial evidence at the time. So, whilst there were mistakes, there were some positives that came out of it as well.”

Judith and her husband John found Una lying dead in a pool of blood, on Sunday, 13 January, 2013, with her clothes burnt.

The curtains were still pulled and her body had been lying there since the previous evening.

They told police that it was odd there was no money in her purse because she regularly drew out a few hundred pounds to pay for odd jobs around the house or even just to bung a few quid to people who had done favours for her.



When the murder investigation belatedly got underway, a few names kept being bandied around, within the close-knit community, as Una’s likely murderers.

It was said that Damon Loates and Mark Coleman tried to steal her money and stabbed her and set her on fire. She had fallen out with her gardener over a tree that was getting cut down.

David Newton, who lived just around the corner, was volatile when drunk and was known to set fire to people’s bins and fences. And even Una’s best friend, Derek Mason, who was left £25,000 in her will, was a suspect because he benefitted financially.



In 2013, forensic scientists took two samples from Una’s fingernails. Her right hand was clenched and lying under her body, so it was protected from any burning. Advances in DNA technology were now to prove crucial.

Iain’s colleague, Detective Inspector Lee Martin Lee, visited the forensic lab where the nails and some of her clothing had been kept.

“Within DNA testing there is a profile known as Y-STR which is the male gene,” Lee explains. “That technique is getting stronger and stronger as the years move on. It can assist with pointing towards a certain bloodline.”

Forensics found a Y-STR result under Una’s fingernails which gave them a positive match to an original suspect – David Newton.



Now, all of Newton’s male relatives needed to be swabbed for DNA, as they shared the same Y-STR and to be eliminated from the enquiries. This was carried out and all of them made statements to say that they had not been in the vicinity of the crime scene at the time of the murder.

But this DNA evidence was not going to be enough for the team to be able to get a prosecution against David Newton. They also needed to build a strong circumstantial case.

Several of Newton’s family painted a dark picture of him. His daughter told detectives she didn’t like the way her dad treated her mum, Janet, throughout her life and added that her dad had ruined her childhood.

Once Janet passed away she told her father that she doubted she would ever see him again.

His brother-in-law recalled Newton hitting Janet and leaving a large bruise over her eye.



Iain and Lee re-watched a 2013 police interview with Janet, where she said her husband was an alcoholic. She also remarked that he had once gone to a locksmith for Una Crown, for new keys, because her back door lock was damaged.

Had he got an extra door key cut for himself so that he could simply let himself on that fateful day?

In his original 2013 interview, David Newton said his usual routine on a Saturday was to go to the ex-services club to play snooker. When asked if he went there again after Una was murdered, he replied, “No, I don’t think so. I didn’t have any money.”

A look back at CCTV footage from the service men’s club on Sunday 13th, the day Una was found dead, shows Newton at the bar, his snooker cue resting on the wall, taking out a large wad of notes from his wallet – unusual for somebody largely on benefits.



The following day he is seen depositing money in his bank. When questioned at the time how he came about suddenly being flush with money, he said his wife had given it to him. But, in her police interview in 2013, she denied that she had.

As well as being an aggressive alcoholic and arsonist, Newton was a voyeur, according to some.

One neighbour told police how he had just turned up at her house one day and she said she was getting ready to go out. Turning away to her bedroom, she walked off, telling him to let himself out. But the next minute, he was standing by her bedroom door, watching her in her underwear.

With their case against Newton building, officers re-arrested him.



During his new interview, Newton, then 69, replied “no comment” to everything but some key questions and comments clearly make him uncomfortable.

He is told that his neighbour, Jackie Henderson, gave a statement to say that at 8.30pm on the night of Una’s murder, she had just got back from shopping and put her bags down on the path and Newton had fallen over them. She said he appeared drunk. Newton is asked, “Was that erratic behaviour down to the fact that you had just come from Una’s bungalow, having murdered her, in a drunken state?

“Eight people from your male lineage have all given statements to say they were not in the vicinity of Una’s bungalow from 12 January 2013. The only person from the male lineage who was seen, 25 metres from Una’s property, was you, on the night she was murdered.”

Now, with enough to prosecute, David Newton was finally brought to trial and on 13 February 2025, he was found guilty of the murder of Una Crown and given a life sentence.

“I thought we had a really good case but that the problem we had was in the jury hearing about the mistakes that were made back in 2013,” says Iain.



“The jury was out for nearly 29 hours. It was really stressful, because that’s a long time. Newton remained emotionless throughout the trial and his sentence.

“It was a hugely emotional moment for the family and for me when the verdict came in. It was 11 years of waiting and one of my proudest days in policing.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Everyone in the force knew about this case because justice had not been done for Una. Now it has. And her family were, at last, allowed to move on with their grieving process.”

24 Hours in Police Custody: The Cold Case Murder, airs on Channel 4, on Monday 13 April and Tuesday 14 April.

News.title: All the Tube strike dates confirmed so far as 12 DAYS of chaos to hit entire network – starting next week
News.content:
COMMUTERS will face 12 days of travel chaos with Tube strikes expected to hit the entire network from next week.

A series of strikes are due to take place over the next three months, wreaking havoc on the London Underground.



The strikes, which will last for 24 hour periods, are a response to disputes over hours, the Rail, Maritime and Transport (RMT) Union announced.



The disruption follows the introduction of a compressed four-day working week for tube drivers, according to the RMT Union.

Union members have cited concerns relating to shift lengths, unacceptable working time arrangements, transfer and allocation processes, and the potential impact on fatigue and safety.

Industrial action was due to take place in March but was suspended after progress in talks with Transport for London.

RMT confirmed around 1,800 of its members were involved in the dispute.

Now, strikes are set to go ahead on twelve separate days spread over the course of April, May and June.

They will run over a 24-hour period from midday to midday the following day.

However, disruption is expected to continue into the afternoons and evenings on those days.

The tube strikes are scheduled to take place on the following dates:



21–22 April (12:00pm Tuesday to 11:59am Wednesday)

23–24 April (12:00pm Thursday to 11:59am Friday)

19–20 May (12:00pm Tuesday to 11:59am Wednesday)

21–22 May (12:00pm Thursday to 11:59am Friday)

16-17 June (12:00pm Tuesday to 11:59am Wednesday)

18-19 June (12:00pm Thursday to 11:59am Friday)

And while reduced services will be run, the strikes are expected to disrupt the entirety of the Tube network.

The Elizabeth line and London Overground are not expected to be directly impacted, though both will be busier than usual if the strikes go ahead.

When the Tube is down, bus and National Rail services generally offer alternative routes across the city.

E-bike hire schemes proved particularly popular during the strikes in September 2025.

News.title: I cheated death three times surviving poisoning, tsunami terror and a horror smash… doctors are shocked I’m alive
News.content:
MOST people would feel lucky to survive one near death experience – but somehow Soulla Demetriou has beaten extraordinary odds three times.

And now the 46-year-old admits: “I don’t know how many lives I have left.”





Revealing how she miraculously survived a string of terrifying experiences, Soulla, who now lives in Ibiza, told The Sun: “I have had quite a few traumatic experiences in my life. It’s like a horror film that keeps playing in my mind.”

As a child growing up in Surrey her entire family was almost wiped out by toxic carbon monoxide poisoning which was only discovered when they all fell dangerously ill on the same night.

Soulla was just 11 years old when her baby sister Sophia started having seizures.

Within hours her mother Ann became temporarily paralysed while Soulla, disorientated and suffering crippling headaches, collapsed and tumbled down the stairs.

And when they all arrived at hospital in an ambulance together on that fateful night, doctors were astounded that any of them were still alive given their oxygen levels had plummeted so alarmingly low.

“In our family home for months, actually possibly even years, in retrospect, we had been suffering different health problems, like very severe headaches,” recalled Soulla.

“One of my sisters was hospitalised with random symptoms of nausea, fainting, dizziness, and then my little sister who is 11 years younger than me, started having seizures when she was a baby.

“Over a period of about six months, she always had them very early in the morning.





“And so the doctors were wondering, is it epilepsy? My parents were trying to decide whether they had to give her medication which, as far as I’m aware, is not a decision to take lightly.

“She was taken to hospital a few times and, on one of the occasions when my little sister had a seizure, my parents actually said, ‘Can you test for carbon monoxide?’

“But there was a blood test that went missing and, unfortunately, carbon monoxide goes out of your blood stream very quickly so by the time they realised they hadn’t got the blood, it was too late to test. The next time she had a seizure was when all our levels were dangerously high.

“Our oxygen was so low.”

Although she is one of four daughters, only Soulla and Sophia were at home with their parents William and Ann on the night of the near-fatal incident. Fortunately, the older two girls were away studying.

She added: “Sophia’s bedroom was above the boiler room, and one night she had a massive seizure that woke us all up.

“And then it all went a bit crazy, because my mum was left temporarily paralysed, because her carbon monoxide levels were so high. I had a room in the attic and I fell down the stairs and cracked my skull and passed out.

I don’t know how many lives I have left at this point, but if we’re going on cat lives, I think I should start taking care Soulla Demetriou

“My dad dragged us all out of the house and called an ambulance. At this point, because the whole family was sick, he was fairly sure, without knowing 100 per cent, that we were being poisoned. Something’s happening.

“We were all taken to hospital together and they didn’t really know what to do with us at the time, because they don’t normally have people come in with that level of carbon monoxide poisoning.



“We were in hospital on oxygen for 48 hours, because there’s not much else they could do.

“My dad was also a heavy smoker but I think the adrenaline kept him alive so he could get us all out of the house. My little sister saved our lives by waking us up by having a seizure.

“We were extremely, extremely lucky, because with that much carbon monoxide, most people would have just died in their sleep.

“We were moments away from death, they said to us.

“It was a very traumatic experience, and it was probably my first experience of PTSD.

“But at the time, there wasn’t really any treatment, not through anyone’s fault. We just survived it and that felt like a miracle. We were very grateful to be alive but then we carried on with our lives.

“Within a few years I was having a lot of anxiety. That sense of inner safety was really ruptured and I’d have flashbacks of that moment when my sister was unconscious for a really long time while we waited for the ambulance – not knowing if she was dead or alive.”

Holiday terror

Years later the closely-bonded family shared a trip of a lifetime to Sri Lanka but during their 2004 holiday the deadly Boxing Day tsunami struck, killing more than 31,000 people.

Soulla, who had been having therapy for panic attacks, was left stranded on the third floor of their hotel while William was miles out to sea on a deep sea fishing trip with her then boyfriend and her older sister’s partners.



For hours, as buildings collapsed around them, they had no idea if the four men were dead or alive.

She said: “Again, it’s a kind of double-edged experience of being very lucky but also still going through an extremely challenging, terrifying experience.

“At first we didn’t really understand what was going on. We were in the restaurant on the third floor but then the water started rising to our level and people on surfboards were jumping inside, to get out of the water.

“There was a phone blackout. There was this sense of terror, and no idea what’s going to happen next.

“When it’s nature, it’s so much bigger than you and we were like sitting ducks with no idea if the wave would come back. We just had to wait.

“We couldn’t get hold of my dad all day, and there was nothing we could do. It was just shock and utter terror, and this panic.

My little sister asked me, ‘Are we just very unlucky?’ But I think we are really lucky actually because we keep surviving things that other people haven’t Soulla Demetriou

“Obviously I was very distressed about not seeing my partner and just feeling so helpless.

“I remember going down to the hotel manager, and everyone’s panicking, but just after sunset suddenly there they were, covered in mud but alive, and that, again, was like a miracle.



“They’d been lucky, because no fish had bitten – we now know that was because of the tsunami – and so they had turned to sail further out.

“Of course, it was kind of a race against the wave, against being swallowed back into the depth of the sea but being further away from the shore was what saved them.”

Even after the family was reunited they struggled to celebrate amid the devastation.

Soulla added: “There was so much gratitude, but there was death everywhere. We wanted to leave, but there were people who had lost everything.

“It was so traumatic, we felt so helpless. We bought sacks of rice and baby bottles, and took them to the camps, but there were just piles of bodies and people wearing rescue blankets.

“When we did eventually get on a plane, it was full of empty seats.

“It was very palpable, the enormous privilege of being able to leave alive, while all these people were devastated by trauma and loss.”



Days later, Soulla was back at her advertising job in London, but unable to focus.

She said: “We had our Monday status meeting and I was looking around thinking this makes no sense, this does not matter. And that really fuelled me to make a change in my life.”

Soulla ditched the corporate world and went travelling around South America and South East Asia, retrained as a yoga teacher and is now running retreats helping people change how they live, think and feel.

She eventually settled in Ibiza but two years ago near-tragedy struck yet again.

“I was kite surfing when a gust of wind picked up very suddenly and lifted me up and smashed me into a variety of very hard things before throwing me into a building, and then I dropped, like a stone to the ground,” she added.

“I had internal organ damage and was in hospital for a month.

“Again, I had a diagnosis of PTSD from that. But I think what was really interesting to me was that I was better resourced this time. Even as I was waiting for the ambulance to arrive, I was thinking, ‘Okay what are the tools I need?’

“Because I didn’t know at that point how serious the injuries were. I couldn’t breathe, I was in agony, I had a bad head injury, neck injury, spine and ribs.



“My little sister asked me, ‘Are we just very unlucky?’ But I think we are really, really lucky actually because we keep surviving things that other people haven’t.

“I don’t know how many lives I have left at this point, but if we’re going on cat lives, I think I should start taking care!”

Now Soulla has published an inspiring new book called You Have Always Been Enough: A Healing Guide to Self-Love and Inner Freedom which reflects what she has learnt along the way.

She explained: “I wouldn’t say there’s one specific moment that led to the book, it has been very much informed by my own personal journey – a culmination of many different moments which led to a lot of pain, suffering and emotional challenges in my life.”

You Have Always Been Enough by Soulla Demetriou is available from Harper Collins now £16.99.

News.title: How Trump is blockading Strait of Hormuz with destroyers, sonar ships, suicide minesweepers & 5,000 Marines ready to go
News.content:
DONALD Trump has unleashed a mighty armada of destroyers, sonar ships and minesweepers after vowing to block the Strait of Hormuz.

The US military has today started taking over the vital shipping lane as Iran refuses to open the waterway and accept a peace deal.





Furious Trump has vowed to stop “any and all ships trying to enter, or leave, the Strait” – through which some 20 per cent of the world’s oil passes.

If successful, a blockade could spell disaster for the Islamic Republic, cutting off its oil and gas exports and therefore crippling its economy.

It has now set the stage for an extraordinary showdown as Washington and Tehran wrestle for control over the chokepoint – with a fragile ceasefire hanging by a thread.

Former CENTCOM commander marine general Frank McKenzie told The Sun: “We have been working for years on plans to take control of the straits area and operate further inland if necessary.”

US Central Command confirmed the blockade will impact maritime traffic entering and exiting Iranian ports as it cuts off the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea after talks over the weekend failed to reach a breakthrough.

Now three lightly armed minesweepers equipped with special sensors are clearing passages through the contested waterway for oil tankers to resume traffic.

Flanked by at least two destroyers, the sweepers will be able to detect mines planted by Iran using small boats in the opening days of the war.



Small aluminium frigates known as Littoral Combat Ships designed to operate close to shore in the Gulf’s shallow waters are carrying highly sensitive AQS-20 sonar to detect mines.

Mines are triggered acoustically by unmanned Influence Sweep Systems -surface vehicles that use simulated magnetic, electric, and acoustic signatures to find sea mines.

Underwater drones measuring 38ft long and MH-60 Seahawk helicopters off Littoral Ships USS Canberra, USS Santa Barbara and USS Tulsa will be scouring waters miles away from the motherships.

Mines that could be floating, tethered by chains or hidden on the sea floor will be located and destroyed.

It comes as the IRGC yesterday issued chilling threats against US ships moving into the narrow 20-mile straits, warning “all vessels in the Oman Sea” to “not to get any closer than ten miles because we will open fire”.



Most of Iran’s navy has been destroyed by the past month’s incessant air strikes that have sunk all its frigates, drone carriers and submarines.

But the bloodthirsty Revolutionary Guard still has hundreds of fast attack Taregh speedboats mounted with short-range missiles and crude rocket propelled grenades.

Concealed along nearby islands and coastal cliffs, they are primed to pounce on the minesweepers.

Hundreds of fighter jets off the aircraft carrier Abraham Lincoln and nearby US bases are flying 24-hour sorties over the waterway to safeguard the minesweeping efforts, however.



But if air cover and gunfire from destroyers prove insufficient to neutralise IRGC threats, Trump has an ace up his sleeve.

Up to 5,000 Navy Seals and Marines already stationed in the region could be deployed – dropping at night by helicopters from Amphibious attack ships to clear islands and coastal missile emplacements.

Sweeping the mines also allows larger US warships to move up into the Persian Gulf to blockade Iranian ports, lay siege and possibly take the key oil terminal on Kharg Island.

Trump has hinted he is ready to do it following the breakdown of weekend peace talks in Pakistan.

The Sun previously told how plans had been drawn up for Trump’s 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit to storm vital island fortresses to unlock the Strait of Hormuz.



Trump has had his crosshairs firmly set on Iran‘s main oil terminal on Kharg Island – where 95 per cent of its oil is shipped.

Floating hospitals, hovercrafts & drone lasers: Trump’s force ready to raid islands Exclusive by Katie Davis WARSHIPS the size of football fields equipped with hospitals and drone lasers have been deployed as Donald Trump gears up to seize Iran’s key islands. Thousands of marines have been arriving in the war-torn region as the US president mulls whether to unleash a ground invasion. The Sun told how plans had been drawn up for Trump’s 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit to storm vital island fortresses to unlock the Strait of Hormuz. But now the Pentagon has given its clearest sign yet of invasion intentions after ordering prefabricated bunkers for island occupations, sources say. Guarded by ruthless IRGC agents armed to the teeth, insiders have warned wrestling these islands from Iran’s grip could be an extremely bloody battle. IRGC island garrisons, gunboats and naval drones are so far being decimated by bunker-busting air bombardments as well as low-flying Apache helicopters and A-10 Thunderbolt jets. But marines – trained to seize and fortify small islands – could encounter intense barrages of Iranian missiles and killer drones launched from virtually anywhere on Iran’s mainland. Iran’s parliament speaker, ex-IRGC officer Bagher Ghalibaf, has threatened to “rain down fire” on any invading US forces. US Army War College professor Evan Ellis told The Sun: “Marines could become a drone magnet.” Additional Marine Expeditionary Units (MEU) with logistical support vessels are now on the way from bases in California to bolster any capture efforts – putting muscle on Trump’s threat to capture Kharg. The 11th Amphibious Ready Group with the landing dock support vessels and 2,500 Marines is more than halfway across the Pacific, making a brief stop in Hawaii this week It’s joining the 31st MEU, with the same number of troops already on station around the Hormuz on USS Tripoli. Reinforcements are due to arrive in the Middle East theatre soon – including a converted container ship equipped with an on board hospital of more than 100 beds. Large numbers of wounded are expected in what could be a “dangerous” mission to gain control of the world’s main oil shipping lands being choked by the IRGC. READ MORE HERE

He suggested earlier this month he could be on the precipice of unleashing his crack squad of marines, saying: “I am considering taking Kharg.”

Other small islands with outsized importance under Tehran’s control also have a red ring around them – as seizing them would break the regime’s stranglehold over the Strait of Hormuz.

Reopening the waterway has become Trump’s top priority since the IRGC started laying mines and firing missiles at oil tankers to block the 19-mile Strait.

But the president had warned he was prepared to walk away from Iran and leave other nations to police the waterway.



He threatened the US “won’t be there to help you anymore” – and said he could end the war with or without a deal.

It could, however, be that Trump was buying time to prepare for a ground invasion after more than a month of diminishing Iran’s capabilities to fight off any daring raid.

Navy Seals, assault submarines and stealth helicopters will be preparing for the sign off on the “dangerous” mission – and cut off the murderous regime’s economic jugular once and for all.

Kharg Island – where 90 per cent of Iran’s oil is stored and shipped from – could become the battleground where Trump checkmates Iran’s crumbling regime.



Oil exports make up around 40 per cent of Iran’s budget, and seizing this tiny five-mile island from the clutches of barbaric clerics would throttle its ability to fund weapons wreaking havoc across the Middle East.

And Iran would no longer be able to bankroll bloodthirsty proxy groups, including Hezbollah or the Houthis – or its nuclear scheme.

For now, Trump’s blockade is in action, with US Central Command warning any Iranian-linked vessel daring to break into the waterway would be subject to “interception or capture”.

It added that the blockade will apply to all regardless of flag, although it will only be enforced “partially” on ships going to and from Iranian ports.

The regime previously branded Trump’s threat as “ridiculous and laughable” – with Iran’s Revolutionary Guard claiming the strait would remain within its grasp.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

But today Tehran appeared to change its tune, with a military spokesperson saying the restrictions amounted to “piracy” and that no port in the Persian Gulf would be safe while Iran is under siege.

Sir Keir Starmer today defiantly ruled out British involvement in the closure, adding the UK will not get “dragged in” to the Iran war.

News.title: Our neighbour built ugly second house in his garden using ‘loophole’ – now he must tear it down… he’s mocked the system
News.content:
BRICK BUST Our neighbour built ugly second house in his garden using ‘loophole’ – now he must tear it down… he’s mocked the system

A DEVELOPER who built a second house in his back garden has been ordered to tear down the “out of character” structure.

Daniel Rayan built the unsightly bungalow without planning permission, with neighbours accusing him of “making a mockery” of planning rules.





Rayan, director of developer Fervid Homes, bought the three-bed detached house in Poole, Dorset for £465,000 in 2022.

He was granted permission to extend the home, turning it into an expansive 5-6 bedroom house.

An old garage and workshop in the garden were also ripped down.

But eagle-eyed neighbours scuppered his further plans for the property, reporting him to local authorities for the illegal construction of a large outbuilding in the garden.

Photos of the property show a square brick building plonked in the garden of the detached home.

The two-bedroom bungalow, built without planning permission, was midway through construction, with ugly planks of plywood and timber frame on show.

Council documents said the structure was not “sympathetic to local character” of properties on the same road.



“It is concluded that the proposal does not preserve the character

and appearance of the street scene nor wider surrounding area,” the decision states.

It added: “Taking into consideration, the surrounding area is characterised by traditional in design properties, it would be considered that the newly built dwelling, due to its contemporary design is not in keeping with pattern of development nearby.”

Neighbour Sally Spiers said the site would still be “cramped and constrained” and there would not be garden space for the occupants of the house.

In comments on the lawful development certificate application, she pointed out the new construction had “changed and increased the existing footprint of the two outbuildings”.

After neighbours reported the illegal construction work, Rayan tried to apply for retrospective planning permission.



That planning application claimed the bungalow would be used as a granny annexe for elderly family members.

But locals said the developer was “making a mockery” of the planning system.

They claimed he was trying to exploit loopholes to maximise the number of renters he could fit in the home.

In planning documents, Rayan claimed the property was a family home, but neighbours insisted it was being used as an HMO (house of multiple occupancy).

When permission was refused, Rayan tried to claim the outbuilding would be used as a gym, study and garden room.



But neighbours again objected to the application for a certificate of lawful development – which had now been refused as well.

A planning officer for Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole Council said there was “very limited evidence” to show the proposed building was genuinely required for the “purposes of being incidental to the enjoyment of the dwelling house”.

She said the footprint of the original main property before the extensions was about 60 sq metres, which meant the footprint of the outbuilding would be bigger than the original house.



The officer also found the bungalow divided the garden into two sections, with the only access to the back of the garden through the new building and that it was 20cm too tall to be allowed under permitted development.

She said: “It is not justified why such a big building would be needed for a gym, study and a garden room.

“Cumulatively, it would be considered that combination of the excessive footprint of the proposed outbuilding together with its siting and subdivision of the external amenity space for occupiers of the dwelling on site, would not appear to be incidental to the enjoyment of the dwelling house.”

Rayan has seven months to tear the building down or he could be taken to court by the local council, unless he appeals the decision.

In written objections to Rayan’s second attempt to gain permission for the unsanctioned outbuilding, Richard Dymott, another neighbour, cast doubt on the stated use for the bungalow.



He said: “The applicant has tweaked his plans to include a gym and garden room and seek approval via permitted development.

“This is yet another example of the applicant using his professional understanding of planning loopholes to get ancillary, rentable rooms into this plot.

“It’s hard to see how a gym and garden room would be utilised by the current residents of his HMO.

“It’s quite clear the use would be changed at later date if the planning officer ignores all the evidence and chooses to approve.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I’d also like to point out that building height along Camelia way is over 2.9 metres and would therefore not fall under permitted development.”



Richard’s damning objection concluded: “Nothing in the new application changes the physical reality that the garden has been unacceptably reduced to squeeze in this new cottage.”



The Sun had contacted Daniel Rayan for comment.

News.title: Tragedy as Tommy Verbickas, 6, dies after third cancer battle
News.content:
Tragedy as Tommy Verbickas dies aged just 6 after his third cancer battle

Tommy Verbickas, from Sale, Greater Manchester, was just two years old when he was diagnosed with Wilms tumour — a form of kidney cancer — after medics found a mass

View 3 Images Tommy Verbicka has passed away after three cancer fights (Image: MEN MEDIA)

A six-year-old boy has died after his third cancer battle.

‌



Tommy Verbickas was first diagnosed with cancer in February 2022 at just two years old when doctors found a 2.3kg mass on his left kidney. Medics discovered the toddler had Wilms tumour — a form of kidney cancer — and the brave youngster had to undergo chemotherapy and surgery.

‌



The little boy, from Sale, Greater Manchester, rang the end-of-treatment bell in November 2022, before sadly relapsing twice and facing cancer for a third time. He has now passed away, his family has said.

‌



Relatives added they hope he is "flying high, dancing through the rainbows." They said: "Our special boy Tommy we hope you're flying high, dancing through the rainbows. Until we meet again our precious boy."

3 View 3 Images Tommy is pictured with his parents, who are from Sale in Greater Manchester (Image: PA Real Life) 3 View 3 Images Tommy was described as the 'most amazing, bravest and courageous little boy' (Image: PA Real Life)

‌



Earlier this week, the family posted about Tommy's condition and how sad they were that they wouldn't have more time with him. They said: "Tommy is still fighting, just as he has done for the past four years. It all feels so unbearably unfair, especially with how quickly everything is happening. I truly believed we’d have more time - time for one last trip to the beach altogether, another battle royale on his PS5, and simply for him to give his dog one more cuddle.

"Watching your precious child fade before your eyes is a pain no parent should ever have to endure. It’s the most heartbreaking kind of helplessness.He is genuinely incredible, and with every breath he takes, he keeps showing just how strong and determined he is."

In an post on April 4, Tommy's mum spoke about how the cancer in his lung had rapidly progressed and how his condition was deteriorating, calling it "the hardest thing we've ever faced," Manchester Evening News reports.

‌



Since his passing, tributes and kind words have flooded in for the "most amazing, bravest and courageous little boy" who showed "so much strength and bravery."

Karen Harrison said: "Tommy the most amazing, bravest and courageous little boy who we love so much. Words can’t describe how we feel right now.

"But we know he will be the brightest star shining in the sky tonight and always. We will never forget him and his cheeky ways and that he still called me Mrs Harrison after 4 years."

Article continues below

Another tribute said that Tommy had 'fought a fight no child ever should'. Jill Stephens said: "He fought a fight no child ever should, but boy did he fight. You gave him everything, every chance, every bit of love. We will always carry him with us, and we will now help carry you through life ahead."

News.title: Donald Trump deletes 'unhinged' Jesus Christ AI image after sparking outrage
News.content:
Donald Trump deletes 'unhinged' Jesus Christ AI image after sparking outrage

Donald Trump was earlier slammed for his 'outrageous blasphemy' after uploading the AI-generated image - which depicted him as a Jesus Christ-like figure healing a sick man

View 2 Images Donald Trump has deleted the AI-generated image (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Donald Trump has deleted an AI-generated image he posted to Truth Social which depicted him as a Jesus Christ-like figure.

‌



In the post, the US president was shown standing with a glowing, divine light from his hands while healing a man in a hospital bed as a demon floats in the background.

‌



The image, which came as Trump launched a shocking attack against Pope Leo, sparked outrage amongst some of his most high-profile Christian supporters.

‌



Megan Basham, a reporter at the conservative Daily Wire, slammed the president for his "OUTRAGEOUS blasphemy," while Isabel Brown, a host on the same outlet, called the image "disgusting and unacceptable".

View 2 Images The image sparked outrage (Image: @realDonaldTrump)

"Nothing matters more than Jesus," she added. "This post is, frankly, disgusting and unacceptable, but also a profound misreading of the American people experiencing a true and beautiful revival of faith in Christ."

‌



Basham demanded Trump to take the photo down immediately. "I don't know if the President thought he was being funny or if he is under the influence of some substance or what possible explanation he could have for this," she said.

"Take this down immediately and ask for forgiveness from the American people and then from God".

On Sunday, Trump posted a lengthy social media rant slamming the pope before telling reporters: "I'm not a fan of Pope Leo". His comments came after the pope suggested a "delusion of omnipotence" was fuelling the US-Israel war in Iran.

Article continues below

"Pope Leo is WEAK on Crime, and terrible for Foreign Policy," the president wrote in a scathing Truth Social post, adding: "I don't want a Pope who thinks it's OK for Iran to have a Nuclear Weapon."

"I like his brother Louis much better than I like him, because Louis is all MAGA," Trump said. "He gets it, and Leo doesn't!"

This is a breaking news story.

News.title: OJ Simpson's 'hypothetical confession' to murder resurfaces after death anniversary
News.content:
OJ Simpson's 'hypothetical confession' to murder resurfaces after death anniversary

O.J. Simpson died aged 76 two years ago, with his his family confirming at the time the former NFL star had been battling prostate cancer

View 2 Images (Image: Fox)

O.J. Simpson's controversial 'Lost Confession' regarding murder has resurfaced.

‌



Two years ago this month, the controversial 76-year-old former NFL player died from prostate cancer.

‌



The family of Simpson announced his passing via social media at the time, releasing a statement: "On April 10th, our father, Orenthal James Simpson, succumbed to his battle with cancer. He was surrounded by his children and grandchildren. During this time of transition, his family asks that you please respect their wishes for privacy and grace." Simpson's fight with prostate cancer, had become known to the public earlier that year.

‌



Back in 1994, Simpson was taken into custody as a suspect in the killings of his former wife Nicole Brown and her friend Ron Goldman. In proceedings later known as the 'Trial of The Century', the ex-sports icon notably rejected any notions of his involvement and was cleared of the murders in 1995.

However, in a divisive Fox News interview 12 years afterwards, he made an unusual hypothetical 'confession' where he spoke about knives, karate and 'blood', while promoting his new book 'If I Did It'.

View 2 Images OJ Simpson - the man at the center of the Trial of the Century - died two years ago (Image: (Photo by Jason Bean-Pool/Getty Images))

‌



The 2006 conversation with Judith Regan certainly divided audiences, though Simpson insisted his 'recollections' were entirely 'hypothetical', while disturbingly chuckling about his account.

"This is very hard for me to do this because it's hypothetical," he told Regan at the time, before mentioning a pal he referred to as Charlie. "Charlie shows up, a guy I'd recently become friends with and he told me you won't believe what's going on over there [at Nicole's house].

"And I remember thinking whatever going on there has got to stop... We get into the Bronco and go over. Hypothetically we park in the alley... in the hypothetical I put on a cap and gloves."

‌



Simpson then proceeds to disclose that he had always kept a knife stashed in his Bronco - the vehicle made notorious during his widely-covered police chase. He explained: "[I reached under the seat and pulled out] a knife. I always kept a knife in that car for the crazies 'cos you can't carry a gun. And I remember Charlie saying 'You can't bring that' and I didn't but I believe he took it..."

He continues to describe hypothetically entering his ex-wife's Los Angeles home through the back gate, spotting lit candles and hearing music playing, before witnessing Goldman's arrival.

Simpson recounted how he began rowing with him before Brown emerged and they became embroiled in a "verbal fight". He said: "It got a little loud and Nicole had come out and we started having words about who is this guy, what's going on...Charlie followed this guy in and brought the knife. As things got heated Nicole fell and hurt herself and this guy got into a karate thing.

Article continues below

"I said: 'Well you think you can kick my ass?'. I remember I grabbed the knife, I do remember that portion...and to be honest I don't remember anything else except I'm standing there and there's all kind of stuff around... blood." Simpson was adamant that his 2006 analogy was entirely hypothetical, and revisited the matter in 2018, stating: "Listen, if I confessed 12 years ago, you would have heard about it 12 years ago!"

Having pleaded not guilty, Simpson faced a landmark trial, widely referred to as the 'trial of the century', which ran for almost a year. Broadcast live, the case ignited fierce national debate surrounding race, gender, domestic abuse, celebrity justice, and police misconduct, ultimately resulting in his acquittal by a jury.

However, a subsequent civil lawsuit brought by the victims' families held him liable for wrongful death and battery, with the court ordering him to pay $33.5 million in damages. Despite this ruling, American law protected his pension fund from being used to settle the debt.

News.title: Families demand 3 changes to prevent another Southport attack and slam killer's parents
News.content:
Families demand 3 changes to prevent another Southport attack and slam killer's parents

The families of Alice da Silva Aguiar, Bebe King and Elsie Dot Stancombe were murdered when Axel Rudakubana entered the Taylor Swift-themed dance workshop in The Hart Space in Southport

Southport Inquiry finds attack ‘could have been prevented’

Solicitors representing the parents of the three little girls killed at a Taylor Swift dance class have called for real change, adding: “This fight does not end today.”

‌



The families of Alice da Silva Aguiar, Bebe King and Elsie Dot Stancombe have called for three changes, which they say will prevent another attack like the atrocity that cost the girls' lives in Southport, Merseyside. These are for agencies to share key information, measures to minimise risks and for authorities to act on opportunities to intervene.

‌



Chris Walker, Bond Turner solicitor representing the three bereaved families, said: “The Southport murders were not only predictable, they were preventable. Today’s publication of the Southport Inquiry report exposes the scale of the systemic failures that led to the tragedy of July 2024.

‌



“For our families, this has always been about honouring their girls and ensuring no one else endures what they face every day. Their participation in the Inquiry took immense courage, and seeing the extent of the failures in black and white is devastating.

“On behalf of our clients we welcome the report’s clear - though deeply distressing - findings on the profound systemic failures and individual failures, that preceded this attack and the responsibility borne by AR’s parents."

3 View 3 Images Alice da Silva Aguiar died in the attack (Image: PA) 3 View 3 Images Tributes also were paid to Elsie Dot Stancombe (Image: PA)

‌



Southport inquiry finds five major systemic failures to stop murder of three innocent girls READ MORE :

He added: “The Chair’s conclusion that this atrocity would not have occurred had agencies taken ownership of the escalating risk is stark. The report details how concerns were repeatedly passed between organisations in what it describes as an ‘inappropriate merry‑go‑round’ of referrals, case closures and missed opportunities. Information was not shared, risks were minimised, and interventions that could have prevented this attack were not taken.

“Crucially, the Inquiry finds that the attack would have been prevented had agencies acted to a competent level. In relation to parental actions, the report is unequivocal: AR’s parents failed in their responsibility to society. He had not left the house for two years except when armed or seeking to cause harm, yet they allowed him to leave on that day knowing he was likely carrying a weapon.

View 3 Images Bebe King's parents have spokenout (Image: AP)

Article continues below

“We are grateful to the Chair’s 67 recommendations that we will consider over the coming days and weeks, commenting further once it has been fully digested. But let us be clear reforms are required urgently.

“On behalf of the families, we repeat the Chair’s hope that this marks a genuine turning point. Our clients have endured unimaginable loss, and their priority has always been preventing this from happening to another family while seeking individual and systemic accountability. This fight does not end today.

“We call for immediate action, clear accountability and real change - not simply reassurances that ‘lessons have been learned’. The public deserves systems capable of identifying escalating risk, protecting the vulnerable and preventing acts of mass violence. We, alongside our clients, will continue to push for that change until it is achieved.”

News.title: Pope Leo makes history as he visits fastest growing Catholic region in Africa for first time
News.content:
Pope Leo makes history as he visits fastest growing Catholic region in Africa for first time

The Pope has embarked on an 11-day tour of Africa with one country visit that holds deep significance to the head of the Vatican - amid comments made by President Trump

View 2 Images Pope Leo has a personal connection to the place he is visiting (Image: ABACA/Shutterstock)

Pope Leo XIV has made it a 'personal priority' to visit the African nations with the fastest growing number of Catholics.

‌



In an 11-day trip, Pope Leo wants to "turn the world's attention to Africa" according to a senior Vatican official. The tour will reflect Africa's increasing importance to to Catholicism, as the Vatican says a recent survey shows a "remarkable increase" in the number of baptised Catholics on the continent.

‌



Addressing themes of peace, migration and dialogue between religions, more than a fifth of the world's Catholics live in Africa, which is roughly 288 million people - making it one of the fastest growing regions.

‌



In his second major foreign tour since being elected, and becoming history's first US-born Pope, it will include visits to 11 cities in four countries - Algeria, Cameroon, Angola and Equatorial Guinea.

View 2 Images The Pope is currently on an 11-day tour of African regions (Image: Christopher Furlong, Getty Images)

All countries but Algeria are have a large Catholic following, making his visit there the first by any pope. The North African country holds "deep significance" to him, as it's the birthplace of St Augustine, and Pope Leo XIV is the first pontiff from the order that follows his teachings according to BBC.

‌



The ideas of the 4th Century North African theologian, such as community and humility, are what helped shape him in becoming the leader of the Catholic Church, and he will visit the region where he was a bishop, and celebrate Mass there.

He will also have talks with Islamic community, which is a key focus for his visit, aiming to promote Christian-Muslim coexistence at a time when there is global conflict.

The Rector of the Basilica, Father Peter Claver Kogh, told the BBC that he expected Pope Leo would "encourage us in our faith and in our mission to build a new world. A world where there is peace and where people live together in harmony."

‌



There is only a small Catholic community in Algeria made up of around 9,000 people who are mostly foreign compared to the Sunni Muslim community of around 47 million.

"It's wonderful to be able to show that we can be brothers and sisters together, building a society despite our different religions", the archbishop of Algiers, French Cardinal Jean-Paul Vesco said. "And that is what our church has been doing since this country gained independence."

The visit comes after Pope Leo says he will continue to speak out against the Iran war after Donald Trump claimed he wasn't doing a good job. The head of the Catholic Church said the Vatican's appeals for peace and reconciliation are rooted in the Gospel, and that he didn’t fear the Trump administration.

Article continues below

It followed Donald Trump taking aim at the Pope over his claim that the war in Iran is being fuelled by a "delusion of omnipotence”. The Pope also called on political leaders to seek peace.

The US president said on Truth Social that the Pope was "WEAK on crime, and terrible for Foreign Policy". He even claimed: "If I wasn't in the White House, Leo wouldn't be in the Vatican."

Speaking to reporters on board the papal plane, the Pope said: "To put my message on the same plane as what the president has attempted to do here, I think is not understanding what the message of the Gospel is. And I’m sorry to hear that but I will continue on what I believe is the mission of the church in the world today.

News.title: 6 key points from Keir Starmer statement warning the world 'has utterly changed'
News.content:
6 key points from Keir Starmer statement warning the world 'has utterly changed'

Keir Starmer answered questions from MPs in the Commons after his two-day trip to the Middle East last week - The Mirror looks at the key points from his statement

View 4 Images Keir Starmer made a statement in the House of Commons (Image: PA)

Keir Starmer said the Middle East "remains on the edge" after Donald Trump began its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.

‌



The PM told the Commons the UK must meet the conflict in the Middle East “calmly but with strength” as he admitted a two-week US-Iran ceasefire is "highly fragile".

‌



The PM made a statement to MPs after a two-day trip to the Gulf, where he held discussions on plans to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Iran initially blocked the vital shipping lane, which transports around a fifth of the world's oil and gas.

‌



But Donald Trump today began his own blockade of the Strait, with the US President warning Iranian naval ships approaching the US Navy's blockade of the country’s ports will be “eliminated” using the same “quick and brutal” method to destroy drug dealers’ boats.

Oil prices spiked back to more than 100 US dollars (£74) a barrel after US talks with Iran broke down and the US president made his belligerent threat to prevent ships leaving from this afternoon.

Mr Starmer admitted the world we live in "has utterly changed", telling MPs: "As the Middle East conflict shows, once more, the world in which we live has utterly changed, it is more volatile and insecure than at any period in my lifetime, and we must rise to meet it calmly but with strength."

‌



Here's some of the key points from the PM's statement to MPs.

View 4 Images Donald Trump today began his own blockade of the Strait of Hormuz (Image: AP)

1. US blockade

The PM has been leading European efforts to try to re-open the Tehran-blockaded Strait of Hormuz. A US-Iran ceasefire attempting to reopen the Strait has faced cracks since being agreed earlier this week. Since then, Donald Trump started his own blockade of Iranian ports, which begun this afternoon, and threatens to deepen the global economic impact from the Middle East crisis.

‌



Mr Starmer told MPs the Strait of Hormuz has been "shamefully exploited by Iran" during the conflict. Speaking about his trip to the Gulf, he said: "All of the leaders that I met were crystal clear that freedom of navigation is vital and must be restored. No conditions, no tolls and no tolerance of Iran holding the world's economy to ransom, because the impact of Iran's behaviour in the Strait is causing untold economic damage."

Challenged on the US blockade specifically, the PM continued: "We are focusing our efforts on opening in full the Strait of Hormuz because of the damage it's doing to economies around the world, including our own economy. That is why we've been working with other countries at various levels and will bring them together in a summit later this, week. And we, the UK, will not be joining the blockade that the President announced."

2. Strait of Hormuz summit

Keir Starmer told MPs he will this week host a summit with French President Emmanuel Macron, focused on diplomatic efforts to end the conflict in the Middle East and military planning to help shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The Prime Minister told the Commons: “I’ve met UK businesses in energy, shipping, insurance and finance, and they are clear that vessels will not be put through the strait until they are confident that it’s safe to do so. “And that’s why we’re working around the clock on a credible plan to reopen the strait. And I can confirm today that, together with President Macron, I will convene a summit of leaders this week to drive forward the international effort we have built in recent weeks, bringing together dozens of countries to ensure freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. “The summit will be focused on two things. First, diplomatic efforts to bring pressure to bear for a negotiated end to the conflict and for the strait to be opened. Second, military planning to provide assurance to shipping as soon as a stable environment could be established.”

‌



View 4 Images Starmer reiterated that Israel's strikes on Lebanon are "wrong" (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

3. Lebanon must be included in ceasefire

Mr Starmer reiterated that Israel's strikes on Lebanon are "wrong" and called for Lebanon to be included in the ceasefire agreement.

Emily Thornberry, chair of the foreign affairs' committee, told the Prime Minister her "blood ran cold" over Israel's threat to follow "the model in Gaza" in Lebanon as she asked what the UK is doing to ensure a ceasefire in Lebanon.

‌



Mr Starmer responded: "I want to be really clear in relation to that. That should be included in the ceasefire, and we're using every opportunity we can to make that argument. And please, there's some diplomacy at the moment, but those attacks should stop. And it's really important that we're very, very clear about that."

He added: “Diplomacy is the right path, and I welcome the talks taking place this week. Hezbollah must disarm, but I’m equally clear Israel’s strikes are wrong. They are having devastating humanitarian consequences and pushing Lebanon into a crisis.”

4. King's State visit

Mr Starmer insisted it is the right thing for the King's state visit to the US to go ahead next month.

‌



Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey piled pressure on the PM to change course. He asked: "Will the Prime Minister advise the King to cool off his state visit to Washington before it's too late? Because I really fear for what Trump might say or do while our king is forced to stand by his side. We cannot put His Majesty in that position."

Mr Starmer responded: "The relationship between our two countries is very important on a number of levels, and often what the monarchy is able to do through the bonds that they build is reached through the decades... The purpose of the visit is to mark the 250th anniversary of the relationship between our country and the United States, and that's why the visit is going ahead."

View 4 Images The PM insisted it is the right thing for the King's state visit to the US to go ahead next month (Image: AP)

Article continues below

5. Closer relations with Europe

The UK’s response to fighting in Iran will involve “a closer economic relationship” with European governments, Sir Keir Starmer has vowed. The Prime Minister told the Commons: “Britain has been buffeted by crises for decades now, from the 2008 financial crash through austerity, Brexit, Covid, the war that still rages in Ukraine, and the disastrous premiership of (former prime minister) Liz Truss. “The response each time has been to try to return to the status quo – a status quo that manifestly failed working people who saw their living standards flatline and their public services decimated. So this time, Britain’s response must and will be different to reflect the changing world that we live in.” Mr Starmer added the UK’s response would mean “a closer economic relationship with our European allies because Brexit did deep damage to the economy”. He continued: “And the opportunities we now have to strengthen our security and cut the cost of living are simply too big to ignore.”

6. Energy independence vow

Keir Starmer has doubled down on his promise to “make Britain energy independent”, warning that billpayers are “fed up with international events beyond their control pushing up their energy bills”. The Prime Minister told the Commons that “oil and gas will be part of our energy mix for decades to come”. He added: “But we do not set the global price for oil and gas, and households across the country are fed up with international events beyond their control pushing up their energy bills, and I stand with them on that. “So we will go further and faster on our mission to make Britain energy independent, because that is the only way we get off the fossil fuel rollercoaster and take control of our energy bills.”

News.title: 'I lost an organ after fat jabs turned my tongue black'
News.content:
'I lost an organ after fat jabs turned my tongue black'

Sarah-Jayne Crawford, who weighed 19st 9lbs when she started taking Wegovy, was horrified at the side effects

View 5 Images Sarah-Jayne in hospital after taking weight-loss jabs (Image: SWNS)

A woman claims weight loss injections turned her tongue black - and resulted in her requiring gallbladder removal. Sarah-Jayne Crawford, 32, began using Wegovy in August 2024 after her weight reached 19st 9lbs.

‌



The mum-of-one, who wore a size 20 at the time, hoped to lose weight ahead of her wedding day in November 2025 and spent £199 through an online pharmacy for a month's worth of the injections at a 0.25mg dose.

‌



However, 12 weeks - and a further £350 later - after upping the dosage to 1mg, matters took an alarming turn when Sarah started experiencing "sharp pains" in her upper abdomen along with regular vomiting episodes, before discovering one December morning that her tongue had become jet black.

‌



The peculiar symptom prevented her from consuming spicy foods - such as peppers and onions - and was accompanied by intense mouth discomfort and repulsive "egg-smelling" sulphur burps. Seriously concerned, she attended A&E at Antrim Area Hospital, where CT and MRI scans identified "multiple" gallstones obstructing her bile duct, plus diverticulitis - an inflammation of abnormal bulging pouches within the large intestine wall - and she ceased using the injections entirely.

View 5 Images Sarah-Jayne's black tongue after taking Wegovy (Image: SWNS)

In February 2025, she underwent a cholecystectomy to have the organ completely removed following the gallstone discovery. Now, nearly fully recovered and no longer using the jabs, Sarah - who currently weighs 18st 8lbs - remains mystified by the peculiar black tongue symptom, and is raising awareness about the potential hidden risks of weight-loss injections. Sarah, a personal secretary working for the NHS, from Antrim, Northern Ireland, explained: "Wegovy was my last resort. I know a lot of people who are on the jabs and it worked like a dream for them.

‌



"I had been battling my weight for what felt like forever and I was dying to slim before my wedding - but dieting, exercising and starving myself never worked. Before, I had heard stories about the dangers and my friend even joked about gallstones, but when the pain left me unable to leave my bed I knew something was up.

"The black tongue seemed like a cherry on top and a warning of what was to come. Never did I think this would happen to me."

Sarah had "always struggled" with her weight throughout her life. However, it wasn't until her partner Curtis, 30, a mechanic, proposed in September 2022 that it spurred her on to shed a few dress sizes.

‌



Recognising that "traditional methods never worked" for her, Sarah spent £199 via an online pharmacy for a two-month supply of Wegovy at 0.25mg dosage.

"At the start, everything seemed fine," she recalled. "My appetite slowly disappeared and I felt great for the wedding. But I wasn't noticing a huge amount of change."

During the subsequent weeks, Sarah spent an additional £350 on Wegovy and ultimately increased her dosage to 1mg. Yet after 12 weeks on the injections, she began suffering "episodes of intense pain" in her upper abdomen and "bouts of vomiting." The stinging sensation rapidly escalated into an "excruciating" trapped wind feeling, leaving her confined to bed. Within just 24 hours, the mum was horrified to find her tongue had turned black – and discovered she could no longer tolerate spicy food.

‌



View 5 Images Sarah-Jayne was shocked by her symptoms (Image: SWNS)

"It all happened so quickly," Sarah said. "It went from really sharp pains that were enough to leave me bedbound, to having sulphur burps, that smelt of egg, and a black tongue. It was terrible. I have a child, so it was very difficult to take time off work.

"But the pain was so unbearable I couldn't walk. I would rather give birth to five kids at the same time than go through with the pain again."

‌



According to the National Center for Biotechnology Information, semaglutide – the active ingredient in Wegovy, which enhances glucose regulation and weight reduction – is recognised for causing dry mouth, halitosis (bad breath) and sulphur-scented burps resulting from delayed digestion – and can allegedly lead to a black-coated tongue.

Alarmed, Sarah immediately discontinued the injections and attended A&E at Antrim Area Hospital, where emergency MRI and CT scans revealed she had numerous gallstones obstructing her bile duct – putting her at risk of developing pancreatitis. She was scheduled for a total cholecystectomy – a surgical procedure to remove the gallbladder – on 10 February 2025, with her surgeon advising her to cease using Wegovy to safely undergo the anaesthetic.

"By this point, I was 18 stone and had hardly lost any weight," she said. "The procedure was about an hour and I cracked on with the recovery. I'm slowly transitioning back to normal and eating more food now - but I'm still far from normal."

‌



View 5 Images Sarah and her son (Image: SWNS)

More than a year on, Sarah has got married and currently weighs 18 stone 8lbs. After stopping the injections in December 2024, her tongue has returned to its natural colour. She attributes most of her weight reduction to illness rather than the jabs – and remains baffled as to how Wegovy caused her tongue to blacken, as medical professionals couldn't provide an explanation.

"I did my research and thought I'd be okay," she said. "But it was the complete opposite. It's not worth it. Weight loss jabs are a temporary fix and the dangers aren't obvious.

‌



"I'm proof that anything can happen once you inject yourself and I have now changed my mindset. Please do you research before you commit - I can't stress enough how much women are putting themselves at risk."

View 5 Images Sarah-Jayne started taking Wegovy in August 2025 (Image: SWNS)

A Novo Nordisk spokesperson, a Wegovy manufacturer, stated: "Patient safety is of the utmost importance to us at Novo Nordisk. To ensure healthcare professionals have a detailed understanding of our medicine's safety profile, the adverse reactions we have observed in clinical trials are detailed in our medicine's Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC).

Article continues below

"In the registrational trials for this medicine, cholelithiasis (acute gallstone disease) was reported in 1.6% of patients and led to cholecystitis in 0.6% of people living with obesity treated with semaglutide 2.4 mg.

"For this reason, acute gallstone disease (cholelithiasis) is listed as a "common" potential adverse reaction for Wegovy (semaglutide injection) in the product's UK SmPC and should be considered when patients are being evaluated for this medicine.

"As part of this work, we also monitor reports of adverse drug reactions through routine pharmacovigilance. If you know of someone who might be experiencing side effects from any medicine, we would advise you to report it to your healthcare provider, and via the MHRA Yellow Card Scheme."
